title: Health Assessment & Nursing Skills: Abdominal & Gastrointestinal Assessment
html:
An abdominal and gastrointestinal assessment evaluates pain, distension, bowel activity, nutrition and hydration, elimination, bleeding risk, and change from baseline. Because many organs share the abdominal cavity, one finding rarely identifies the cause. The RN combines the client’s history with inspection, bowel sounds, percussion and light palpation, vital signs, intake and output, stool or emesis characteristics, recent procedures, medications, and trends.

Learning goals

  • Collect a focused gastrointestinal and abdominal history using precise symptom questions.
  • Prepare and position the client for a respectful, accurate examination.
  • Use the abdominal sequence: inspection, auscultation, percussion, then palpation.
  • Describe contour, bowel sounds, percussion notes, tenderness, guarding, and related findings objectively.
  • Recognize bleeding, obstruction, peritoneal irritation, dehydration, and shock warning patterns.
  • Document assessment context, actions, communication, and response.

Begin with stability and urgent symptoms

Observe appearance, position, movement, skin color and moisture, breathing, and responsiveness. Assess airway, breathing, circulation, pain, and vital-sign trends before a routine abdominal examination. Hematemesis, new or worsening black tarry stool or bloody stool, severe or rapidly worsening pain, a rigid abdomen, syncope, hypotension, tachycardia with pallor or diaphoresis, or declining mental status requires prompt assessment and escalation.

Other concerning patterns include progressive distension with vomiting and inability to pass stool or flatus; severe pain out of proportion to examination findings; sudden pain after surgery, procedure, trauma, or anticoagulant use; and a new pulsatile abdominal mass with pain or poor perfusion. Stop the routine sequence, maintain safety, keep oral intake on hold when indicated by orders or emergency protocol, and obtain immediate assistance.

Do not deeply palpate a pulsatile mass
A newly observed or suspected pulsatile abdominal mass—especially with pain, hypotension, syncope, or perfusion change—requires urgent evaluation. Avoid repeated or deep palpation and prioritize circulation, monitoring, and emergency response.

Ask the client to tell the story

Use PQRSTU or a similar structure for abdominal pain: onset, provoking and relieving factors, quality, location and radiation, severity, timing, prior episodes, treatments, associated symptoms, and the client’s concerns. Ask the client to point with one finger to the area of greatest pain. Clarify whether pain is constant, colicky, burning, cramping, pressure-like, related to meals, movement, urination, bowel movements, coughing, or position.

Ask about appetite, early satiety, weight change, swallowing difficulty, reflux, nausea, vomiting, bloating, distension, belching, and food intolerance. For vomiting, record frequency, amount when measurable, color, contents, blood or coffee-ground appearance, triggers, and ability to keep fluids down. Ask about the usual bowel pattern, last bowel movement, stool frequency and consistency, diarrhea, constipation, urgency, incontinence, mucus, blood, black tarry appearance, pale stool, and flatus.

Review abdominal or gastrointestinal conditions, surgeries, ostomies, feeding tubes, recent endoscopy or procedures, travel and exposure history when relevant, alcohol use, pregnancy possibility when clinically appropriate, and family history. Review medications that may affect bleeding, motility, stool appearance, nausea, or mucosa, including anticoagulants, antiplatelets, NSAIDs, iron, bismuth, opioids, antibiotics, laxatives, and supplements. Medication effects may explain a clue but should not be assumed without assessing the complete pattern.

Prepare for comfort, accuracy, and dignity

Explain the examination and obtain consent before touch. Provide privacy and expose only the abdomen from the lower chest to the pubic area as needed while keeping breasts and genitalia covered. Ask the client to empty the bladder when appropriate. Position supine with the head and knees supported to relax the abdominal wall; keep arms at the sides rather than behind the head. Warm the room, hands, and stethoscope.

Observe the face and body for nonverbal pain during the examination. Begin away from the painful area and palpate that area last if the client is stable. Stop if distress increases or the clinical picture becomes urgent. Respect scars, trauma history, cultural needs, and the client’s right to pause or decline nonemergency parts of the examination.

Use the abdominal sequence: I-A-P-P

The abdominal sequence is inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation. Auscultation occurs before percussion and palpation because touching or tapping can stimulate bowel activity and change the sound pattern. This order differs from the common sequence used for many other systems.

Inspect before touching

View the abdomen at eye level and from above with adequate direct and tangential light when available. Describe overall contour and symmetry, localized or generalized distension, movement with respiration, skin color and integrity, scars, striae, lesions, veins, wounds, dressings, drains, tubes, stomas, and visible bulges. Note visible peristalsis or pulsation without manipulating the area.

Inspect an ostomy for location, stoma color and moisture, surrounding skin, appliance seal, and output as relevant. Check tubes and drains for securement, prescribed settings, insertion-site condition, and output. Do not infer bowel function from abdominal shape alone; obesity, pregnancy, posture, muscle tone, ascites, gas, stool, and masses can all change contour.

Auscultate before percussion or palpation

Use the diaphragm of a warmed stethoscope directly on skin with light pressure. Follow the organization’s systematic quadrant sequence, commonly beginning in the right lower quadrant and moving clockwise. Listen for the presence, character, and distribution of bowel sounds. Avoid counting individual sounds as though a single frequency establishes motility; bowel activity is irregular and sounds can transmit across the abdomen.

If sounds are not heard promptly, continue listening for the duration required by current policy and the clinical context before documenting them as absent. A quick listen is insufficient. Describe sounds using approved terms and interpret them with pain, distension, nausea, vomiting, flatus, stool, medications, surgery timing, and intake. Hyperactive, hypoactive, or absent sounds are assessment cues, not stand-alone diagnoses.

Auscultation for vascular bruits uses specific landmarks and technique and should be performed only when indicated and within training and policy. Do not press deeply over a suspected vascular abnormality.

Percuss for distribution, not a diagnosis

Percussion can help distinguish areas of gas, fluid, or denser tissue and estimate borders when part of the trained examination. Move systematically and compare regions. Tympany is commonly heard over gas-filled areas, while dullness may occur over solid organs, fluid, stool, or masses. An unexpected note must be paired with the rest of the assessment; percussion alone cannot determine the cause.

Specialized maneuvers for organ size, ascites, gallbladder, appendix, or costovertebral-angle tenderness require correct indication and technique. Do not repeatedly perform provocative maneuvers on a client with severe pain or instability merely to reproduce a finding.

Palpate gently and leave pain until last

Use the pads and flat surface of the fingers for light palpation, beginning in a nonpainful quadrant. Assess muscle tone, superficial tenderness, guarding, and unexpected masses while watching the client’s face. Ask whether discomfort is caused by pressure and document its location and severity. Voluntary guarding may decrease with relaxation; involuntary rigidity or persistent guarding is more concerning when paired with severe pain or systemic change.

Deep palpation and detailed organ assessment may be outside the routine bedside nursing examination and should be performed only when indicated, trained, and within scope. Avoid deep palpation of a pulsatile mass. Rebound tenderness and other provocative tests can increase pain and should not be repeated casually; communicate already established findings.

Connect the abdomen with hydration, nutrition, and elimination

Assess oral intake, swallowing safety, recent diet, weight trend, mucous membranes, thirst, urine output, orthostatic symptoms, and laboratory data when available. Repeated vomiting or diarrhea can cause volume and electrolyte loss. Reduced urine output, tachycardia, hypotension, dizziness, dry mucosa, delayed refill, weakness, or mental-status change increases concern.

Quantify intake and output when ordered. Describe stool and emesis rather than using only labels such as “normal.” Black stool can occur with iron or bismuth, but a new tarry appearance with weakness, abdominal symptoms, anticoagulant use, or hemodynamic change must be assessed for bleeding. Bright red blood, maroon stool, coffee-ground emesis, or frank hematemesis also requires prompt evaluation based on amount and client status.

Recognize postoperative and device-related change

After abdominal surgery or anesthesia, interpret bowel sounds and elimination with the procedure, medication exposure, pain, mobility, diet advancement, nausea, distension, and passage of flatus or stool. Progressive distension, worsening pain, repeated vomiting, fever, wound change, hemodynamic instability, or lack of expected recovery cues requires timely follow-up. Do not advance intake or manipulate tubes outside orders and policy.

For feeding tubes, drains, urinary catheters, and ostomies, assess the client first, then the device. Verify purpose, prescribed settings, securement, insertion site, output amount and character, skin protection, and ongoing need. A functioning device does not rule out an abdominal complication.

Respect delegation boundaries

Assistive personnel may report stool, emesis, intake and output, weight, appetite, or observed distension and can collect assigned routine data for a stable client according to policy. The RN validates concerning findings, performs the focused abdominal assessment, interprets the pattern, determines urgency, initiates nursing action, communicates change, and evaluates the response. A report of black stool, blood, repeated vomiting, or new distension requires timely RN assessment.

Document findings that another nurse can compare

Record symptoms and onset; pain location, quality and severity; contour and symmetry; skin, scars, devices, wounds and stomas; bowel-sound character and areas assessed; percussion findings when performed; palpation depth and tenderness, guarding or rigidity; stool, flatus and emesis; intake and output; relevant vital signs and position; baseline comparison; interventions; communication; and reassessment.

For example: “1610: New generalized abdominal distension with nausea and two episodes of green emesis, approximately 150 mL total. Reports cramping pain 7/10 and no flatus since morning. Bowel sounds not heard after assessment for the duration specified by unit policy; abdomen firm with guarding, light palpation stopped. BP 94/58, HR 112. Client maintained NPO per postoperative protocol; surgical team and rapid response notified at 1614.” This is more useful than “possible obstruction.”

Clinical example

An assistive team member reports that a client’s stool is “very dark.” The RN assesses the client rather than assuming it is caused by iron. The RN clarifies color and consistency, reviews medication and bleeding risk, asks about pain, weakness and dizziness, checks vital signs and perfusion, observes the stool when available, and communicates promptly if the pattern suggests bleeding. The RN then reassesses after prescribed evaluation or intervention.
